courses.subject: GPGC
courses.title: Politics of Transition And Greater China
courses.description: This course will focus on the political economy of transition of former communist countries and reforming socialist countries, with Greater China situated in this context. It will examine the major political, economic, and social transformations of these countries, and discuss the major patterns of changes.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSSc in Government and Politics (Greater China)
courses.learning_outcomes:
(A) A general understanding of the transformation of post-communist and reforming-socialist countries.
(B) The ability to analyse Greater China's political economy and culture in the above context.
(C) Mastery of the theoretical frameworks and issues related to A and B above.
courses.course_syllabus:
Part 1: Totalitarian and Authoritarian Systems. The Concept of Leninist One-party State

Part 2: Soviet Studies and China Studies on Establishment, Evolution and Reform in State Socialist Systems. The Concept of “Post-Totalitarian Society”

Part 3: Attempts of Market Transitions in the Countries of the “Soviet Block”

Part 4: Historical Dynamics of Market Reforms in the People’s Republic of China

Part 5: Market Reforms in Totalitarian and Authoritarian Systems: What is Common, What is Different?

Part 6: Constellation of Systemic Actors in Totalitarian and Authoritarian Market Reforms Models. Reasons for Chronic Macro Economic Problems in Reformed State Socialism
courses.feedback_evaluation:
An official evaluation of the scope of the course, well-preparedness of the teaching staff, ability of the teaching staff to inspire
students, mode of assessment, and others, will be submitted by students after completing the course.

courses.subject: GPGC
courses.title: Anti-Corruption In Comparative Perspective
courses.description: This course presents an in-depth survey of best practices adopted by governments, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and other stakeholders to eradicate corruption and promote transparency. The course reviews elements in public sector management commonly known as ""good governance,"" the causes and effects of corruption, and undertakes a comparative study of domestic and multilateral anti-corruption efforts.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSSc in Government and Politics (Greater China)
courses.learning_outcomes:
(A) To understand various reasons leading to corruption and to be familar with the history and theories of anti-corruption.
(B) To be able to analyze the origin of corruption from different perspectives.
(C) To appreciate the pros and cons of each anti-corruption method and apply the theories in the local setting.
courses.course_syllabus:
Major concepts and topics to be covered:

Rule of law, accountability; democracy; public service delivery; administrative reform; government-business relations; patronage; kleptocracy; financial scandal; bribery; rent seeking; economic crime, nepotism; clientelism, social values; informal institutions; civil servant salary; professional integrity; transparency; honesty and trust; anti-corruption campaigns, Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC), institutional hindrances to corruption control

courses.subject: GPGC
courses.title: State-Society Relations In Greater China
courses.description:
This course is designed to expose graduate students to major debates over state-society relationships in the study of contemporary Greater China's politics, such as ""the reach of the state,"" citizenship and rights, civil society and democratization.
The course also encourages students to consider how well the state-society paradigm works in Greater China studies.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSSc in Government and Politics (Greater China)
courses.learning_outcomes:
(A) A general understanding of the transformation of contemporory state-society relations in Greater China.
(B) The ability to analyze focal socio-political issues in Greater China with state-society approach.
(C) A basic understanding of the logic of concept formation, concept application and concept transformation in
political science.
courses.course_syllabus:
Topic 1 The Reach of the Maoist State

Topic 2 Workers under Socialism

Topic 3 Understanding the Post-Mao State

Topic 4 Popular Resistance

Topic 5 Workers after Socialism

Topic 6 NGOs and the Civil Society Debate

Topic 7 News Media and Internet

Topic 8 Contemporary Urban Life and the Middle Class

courses.subject: GPGC
courses.title: Environmental Politics of Greater China
courses.description: This course is designed as both an introduction of environmental politics and a sectoral analysis of general politics in the context of contemporary Greater China. On the one hand, it introduces environmental governance and politics in general in the mainland, Hong Kong and Taiwan. On the other hand, it uses the case of environmental politics to teach students about political changes in the three places in the past three decades.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSSc in Government and Politics (Greater China)
courses.learning_outcomes:
(A) Knowledge of the features and challenges of the governing structures in environmental protection in contemporary Greater China.
(B) Application of general comparative politics theories to explain the causes and impact of environmental governance in
Chinese politics in general.
(C) Using evidence from the environmental sector to understand the central theoretical debates on political development。

1. Environmentalism, Political Change and Governance
2. Environmental Governance and Politics in Mainland China
3. Environmental Governance in Taiwan and Hong Kong
4. Environmental Activism
5. Air
6. Waste
7. Field Trip
8. Water
9. Conservation and biodiversity
10. Environmental Diplomacy and Transnational Issues
11. Comparative Analysis and Other Factors

courses.subject: GPGC
courses.title: Political Communication in Practice
courses.description: Political communication is a vital part of the daily work of politicians. They need to share their visions with the public. They need to help people understand complex public policy questions and solutions. They need to rally people to support certain courses of actions. And most important, they need to convince the voters in order to get elected and remain in power. To achieve these, effective communication is very important. This course aims at introducing students the basic theories and practices of political communication. It would explore the ways in which political messages are sent and received so that students can better understand how their lives are shaped, and then have a better reflection of real life politics. Moreover, while political communication becomes a rising profession, this course can provide a basic training to those students who want to begin their careers in this field.
courses.enrollment_requirement: For students in MSSc in Government and Politics (Greater China)
courses.learning_outcomes:
(A) Understand major concepts, ideas and theories in political communication.
(B) Learn basic principles and skills in areas such as speech writing and delivering, election debate, political
advertising, and media handling.
(C) Understand the new political phenomenon of political spinning.
(D) Learn how to apply knowledge taught in the course in real political life.
courses.course_syllabus:
1. Political Communication in the Era of Professionalization
2. Changes in Political News Coverage: Personalization, Conflict and Negativity
3. The Changing Culture and Environment of African Political Communication
4. Professionalism of Political Communication
5. Visual Political Communication
6. Political Marketing
7. Social Media and the Organization of Collective Action
8. News Framing
9. Negative Advertising and Election
